source_text: Quod si uerum est, profecto etiam prouisus sepeliendis corporibus apud memorias sanctorum locus bonae affectionis humanae est erga funera suorum, quoniam, si nonnulla religio est, ut sepeliantur, non potest nulla esse, quando ubi sepeliantur adtenditur. sed cum talia uiuorum solacia requiruntur, quibus eorum pius in suos animus adpareat, non uideo quae sunt adiumenta mortuorum nisi ad hoc, ut, dum recolunt, ubi sint posita eorum quos diligunt corpora, eisdem sanctis illos tamquam patronis susceptos apud dominum adiuuandos orando commendent. quod quidem facere possent, etiamsi talibus locis eos humare non possent. sed non ob aliud uel \'memoriae\' uel (monumenta> dicuntur ea quae insignite fiunt sepulcra mortuorum, nisi quia eos, qui uiuentium oculis morte subtracti sunt, ne obliuione etiam cordibus subtrahantur, in memoriam reuocant et admonendo faciunt cogitari. nam et (memoriae) nomen id apertissime ostendit et (monumentum) eo quod moneat mentem, id est admoneat, nuncupatur. propter quod et Graeci μvημεῑοuocant, quod nos memoriam seu monumentum appellamus, quoniam lingua eorum memoria ipsa, qua meminimus, μvήμη dicitur. cum itaque recolit animus, ubi sepultum sit carissimi corpus, et occurrit locus nomine martyris uenerabilis, eidem martyri animam dilectam commendat recordantis et precantis affectus. qui cum defunctis a fidelibus carissimis exhibetur, eum prodesse non dubium est his, qui cum in corpore uiuerent, talia sibi post hanc uitam prodesse meruerunt. uerum et si aliqua necessitas uel humari corpora uel in talibus locis humari nulla data facultate permittat, non sunt praetermittendae supplicationes pro spiritibus mortuorum, quas faciendas pro omnibus in christiana et catholica societate defunctis etiam tacitis nominibus eorum sub generali commemoratione suscepit ecclesia, ut quibus ad ista desunt parentes aut filii aut quicumque cognati uel amici, ab una eis exhibeantur pia matre communi. si autem deessent istae supplicationes, quae fiunt recta fide ac pietate pro mortuis, puto, quod nihil prodesset spiritibus eorum, quamlibet locis sanctis exanima corpora ponerentur.
thought_title: Burial at a holy memorial helps only through the living's prayerful remembrance
orientation: Augustine has just restated his view on burial and now explains that a burial place at a martyrs' memorial shrine benefits the dead only insofar as it stirs the living to pray for them.
pass_a_gloss: But if this is true, certainly also a place provided for burying bodies at the memorial shrines of the saints is a place of good human affection toward the funerals of one's own, since, if there is some religious duty that they be buried, it cannot be no duty when attention is paid to where they are buried. But when such consolations of the living are sought, by which their pious disposition toward their own may appear, I do not see what helps there are for the dead except for this, that, while they recall where the bodies of those whom they love have been placed, they commend those same persons to those same saints as to patrons, to be helped before the Lord by praying. This indeed they could do even if they could not bury them in such places. But the things which are made as notable tombs of the dead are called either memorial shrines or monuments for no other reason than that they call back into remembrance those who have been withdrawn from the eyes of the living by death, lest they be withdrawn also from hearts by forgetfulness, and by reminding they make them be thought of. For the name memorial shrine shows this most openly, and monument is named from the fact that it warns the mind, that is, reminds it. For this reason the Greeks also call it μvημεῑοv, which we call memorial shrine or monument, since in their tongue the memory itself, by which we remember, is called μvήμη. When therefore the mind recalls where the body of a most dear person has been buried, and the place occurs to it, venerable by the name of a martyr, the affection of one remembering and praying commends the beloved soul to that same martyr. When this affection is shown to the dead by faithful and most dear persons, there is no doubt that it benefits those who, while they were living in the body, merited that such things benefit them after this life. But even if some necessity either does not allow bodies to be buried or does not allow them to be buried in such places, no opportunity having been given, prayers for the spirits of the dead are not to be omitted, which prayers the church has undertaken to make for all who have died in Christian and catholic society, even with their names unspoken, under a general commemoration, so that those for whom parents or children or any relatives or friends are lacking for these things, these things may be shown to them by the one pious common mother. But if those prayers were lacking, which are made with right faith and piety for the dead, I think that it would benefit their spirits nothing, however much lifeless bodies were placed in holy places.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'memorial shrine' for memoria, and the plural here refers to the shrines of the saints.
Augustine distinguishes monumentum from memoria by its etymology from monere, so 'monument' preserves the wordplay.
The glossary requires 'affection' for affectus, and the phrase describes the natural loving disposition toward one's own dead.
Augustine uses the legal metaphor of patrons as advocates; the glossary's 'intercession' is for patrocinium, but here the persons are called patroni.
The glossary requires 'prayerful commending' for commendatio, and the verb here carries the same sense of entrusting the dead to the martyr in prayer.
The glossary requires 'prayer' for supplicatio, and the plural here refers to prayers of entreaty for the dead.

pass_b_english: If this is true, then providing a place for burying bodies at the memorial shrines of the saints is certainly an act of good human affection toward one's own dead. For if there is some religious duty in burying them, there cannot be none when attention is paid to where they are buried. But when such consolations of the living are sought, by which their pious disposition toward their own may appear, I do not see what helps they are to the dead except this: that while they recall where the bodies of those they love have been placed, they commend them in prayer to those same saints, as to patrons, to be helped by them before the Lord. They could do this even if they could not bury them in such places. But the reason why the notable tombs of the dead are called either 'memorial shrines' or 'monuments' is none other than this: they call back into remembrance those who have been withdrawn from the eyes of the living by death, so that they are not also withdrawn from their hearts by forgetfulness, and by reminding they make them be thought of. For the name 'memorial shrine' shows this most openly, and 'monument' is named from the fact that it admonishes the mind, that is, it reminds. This is why the Greeks also call it μνημεῖον, which we call a memorial shrine or monument, since in their language the memory itself by which we remember is called μνήμη. And so when the mind recalls where the body of a dearest one is buried, and the place occurs to it as venerable by the name of a martyr, the affection of the one remembering and praying commends that beloved soul to the same martyr. When this affection is shown to the dead by their dearest faithful ones, there is no doubt that it benefits those who, while they were living in the body, merited that such things would benefit them after this life. But even if some necessity, when no opportunity is given, prevents bodies from being buried at all, or from being buried in such places, prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. The church has undertaken to make these prayers for all who have died in Christian and catholic fellowship, even without naming them, under a general commemoration, so that those who lack parents or children or any relatives or friends to do these things may have them offered by the one pious common mother. But if those prayers were lacking, which are made with right faith and piety for the dead, I think it would profit their spirits nothing, however much their lifeless bodies were placed in holy places.

problems.quote: they commend them in prayer to those same saints, as to patrons who have received them, to be helped before the Lord
problems.source_quote: eisdem sanctis illos tamquam patronis susceptos apud dominum adiuuandos orando commendent
problems.why: Latin 'susceptos' modifies the dead (illos), not the saints: the dead are 'taken up/received' by the saints as patrons, not the saints who have received them. English reverses who receives whom.
problems.fix: they commend them in prayer to those same saints, as to patrons by whom they have been received, to be helped before the Lord
problems.ruling: 'susceptos' modifies 'illos' (the dead): they are received by saints as patrons, not saints who received them.
